symptoms: Small, circular to oval orange-brown pustules (uredinia) scattered randomly across the upper leaf surface.
As the disease matures, pustules turn dark glossy black (telia) and leaf sheaths begin to dry out.
Severe infections cause premature leaf senescence, drastically reducing grain yield and kernel weight.
Wheat___Brown_Rust.causes: Caused by the fungus Puccinia triticina. It thrives in warm, humid weather (15°C to 25°C) with at least 6 hours of continuous leaf wetness from dew or light rain.
treatment: Apply systemic triazole fungicides immediately upon spotting early pustules on the flag leaf.
Prioritize protecting the flag leaf (topmost leaf), as it contributes up to 75% of the grain-filling energy.
Avoid excess nitrogen fertilization during an active outbreak, as dense canopies trap moisture and accelerate spore germination.
prevention: Plant certified rust-resistant wheat cultivars suited for your regional growing zone.
Eradicate volunteer wheat plants and grassy weeds during the off-season to eliminate overwintering green bridges.
Maintain balanced soil nutrition with adequate potassium and phosphorus to strengthen cell wall resistance.
Wheat___Brown_Rust.fungicide: Propiconazole (25% EC at 1 ml/liter of water) or Tebuconazole 25.9% EC. Spray at 10-15 day intervals if weather remains humid.
Wheat___Brown_Rust.recovery_tips: If sprayed early, new emerging leaves will remain green. Boost crop recovery by applying a foliar spray of 2% Potassium Nitrate (KNO3) during the boot stage to aid grain filling.

symptoms: Bright yellow to neon-orange pustules arranged in highly visible, straight parallel stripes along the leaf veins.
Yellow dust (spores) easily rubs off onto fingers, clothing, or farm equipment when brushing past infected plants.
In severe cases, stripes merge into large chlorotic (yellowed) patches, causing rapid dehydration and stunting.
Wheat___Yellow_Rust.causes: Caused by the fungus Puccinia striiformis f. sp. tritici (Stripe Rust). Unlike Brown Rust, Yellow Rust is a cool-weather disease, favoring temperatures between 10°C and 15°C with intermittent moisture.
treatment: Stripe rust spreads exponentially faster than brown rust; initiate chemical sprays at the very first sign of stripe lesions.
Use dual-action strobilurin + triazole premixes for immediate curative knockdown and extended residual protection.
Ensure high water volume (400-500 liters/hectare) during spraying to penetrate deep into the lower wheat canopy.
prevention: Utilize multi-gene adult plant resistance (APR) varieties rather than single-gene resistant varieties.
Alter sowing dates slightly to avoid aligning the vulnerable seedling stage with peak regional spore release periods.
Monitor regional agricultural extension weather alerts during cool, wet spring months.
Wheat___Yellow_Rust.fungicide: Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Cyproconazole 7.3% SC, or Pyraclostrobin + Epoxiconazole applied at recommended agricultural rates.
Wheat___Yellow_Rust.recovery_tips: Yellow rust can destroy a crop within 3 weeks if unchecked. Once halted by fungicides, avoid drought stress by maintaining light, consistent irrigation during heading and flowering.

symptoms: Vibrant green, uniform leaf blades without pustules, lesions, yellow stripes, or necrotic tip burn.
Stems and leaf sheaths are clean and structural turgor is strong.
Normal grain head emergence and flowering progression.
Wheat___Healthy.causes: Optimal soil nutrition, balanced moisture, good field drainage, and absence of fungal pathogen pressure.
treatment: No therapeutic chemical treatment required.
Continue standard agronomic monitoring every 5-7 days.
prevention: Maintain crop rotation schedules (e.g., wheat-pulse or wheat-oilseed rotation).
Apply basal micro-nutrients like Zinc and Boron during soil preparation to maintain natural plant immunity.
Wheat___Healthy.fungicide: None required. Avoid unnecessary prophylactic fungicide applications to prevent fungal resistance buildup.
Wheat___Healthy.recovery_tips: Your wheat crop is in excellent health! Ensure timely irrigation at critical growth stages: Crown Root Initiation (CRI), Flowering, and Grain Filling.

symptoms: Dark brown to black circular spots with concentric rings (target-board appearance) on older lower leaves.
Yellowing of leaf tissue surrounding the dark lesions.
Premature defoliation starting from the base of the plant upward.
Tomato___Early_blight.causes: Caused by the fungus Alternaria solani. It overwinters in infected plant debris and soil, spreading via wind, rain splash, and overhead irrigation.
treatment: Prune and remove infected lower leaves immediately to reduce spore load; sterilize pruning shears between cuts.
Apply protective copper-based fungicides or targeted chemical sprays.
Improve air circulation around plants by staking and spacing appropriately.
prevention: Practice a 2-3 year crop rotation away from solanaceous crops (potatoes, tomatoes, peppers).
Use drip irrigation or soaker hoses instead of overhead watering to keep foliage dry.
Apply organic mulch around the base of plants to prevent soilborne spores from splashing onto leaves.
Tomato___Early_blight.fungicide: Chlorothalonil 75% WP (2 g/liter) or Mancozeb 75% WP. Apply every 7-10 days during humid weather.
Tomato___Early_blight.recovery_tips: Feed recovering plants with a balanced liquid seaweed or compost tea boost. Ensure consistent soil moisture without waterlogging to minimize physiological stress.

symptoms: Large, irregular water-soaked dark green to purplish-brown lesions on leaves and stems.
White fungal growth visible on the underside of leaves during humid mornings.
Rapid browning and shriveling of foliage, emitting a distinct odor of decay.
Tomato___Late_blight.causes: Caused by the water mold oomycete Phytophthora infestans. Thrives in cool, consistently wet, and humid weather conditions.
treatment: Remove and destroy severely infected plant parts immediately; do not put them in compost piles.
Apply systemic oomycete-targeted fungicides as soon as symptoms appear.
In severe neighborhood outbreaks, terminate heavily infected crops to prevent regional windborne spread.
prevention: Plant certified disease-resistant tomato varieties (e.g., varieties with Ph-2 and Ph-3 resistance genes).
Avoid planting tomatoes near potatoes, which act as primary carriers and overwintering hosts.
Ensure full sun exposure and wide planting rows for rapid morning foliage drying.
Tomato___Late_blight.fungicide: Metalaxyl 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP (2.5 g/liter), or Dimethomorph + Pyraclostrobin formulations.
Tomato___Late_blight.recovery_tips: Late blight is notoriously difficult to cure once established. If caught early, prune aggressively into healthy tissue and maintain strict chemical protection on new growth.

symptoms: Target-like concentric dark brown rings on older potato foliage.
Lesions are restricted by leaf veins, giving them an angular, geometric appearance.
Infected tubers develop dark, sunken, leathery dry rot lesions under the skin.
Potato___Early_Blight.causes: Caused by Alternaria solani. Accelerated by nitrogen deficiency, drought stress, and heavy fruiting/tuber load.
treatment: Maintain optimal soil nitrogen and fertility levels to delay natural plant senescence.
Spray foliar fungicides when plants reach flowering stage or upon first lesion appearance.
Allow tubers to mature completely and skin to set before harvesting to prevent harvest bruising.
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed potatoes.
Destroy potato cull piles and volunteer weeds before planting.
Maintain consistent soil moisture through automated irrigation scheduling.
Potato___Early_Blight.fungicide: Azoxystrobin 23% SC or Difenoconazole 25% EC applied at 14-day intervals.
Potato___Early_Blight.recovery_tips: Avoid harvesting potatoes in wet soil. Store harvested potatoes in a well-ventilated, dark, cool curing room at 12°C to 15°C for two weeks to allow skin healing.

symptoms: Pale green to dark brown water-soaked spots surrounded by a pale yellow halo on leaf tips.
Under humid conditions, a delicate white fungal mold forms around the border of lesions on leaf undersides.
Tubers show reddish-brown to purplish irregular sunken discoloration that extends into the flesh as rot.
Potato___Late_Blight.causes: Caused by Phytophthora infestans. Can destroy entire potato fields within days during cool, rainy weather.
treatment: Spray curative translaminar fungicides immediately upon weather warnings.
If more than 10% of foliage is destroyed, desiccate (burn down) potato haulms (vines) using herbicide 2 weeks before harvest to prevent tuber infection.
Do not harvest until vines are completely dead and dry.
prevention: Earth up (hill) potato rows adequately with soil to create a physical barrier between rain-washed spores and developing tubers.
Destroy all infected cull piles, as they are the primary breeding ground for new spring outbreaks.
Potato___Late_Blight.fungicide: Cymoxanil + Mancozeb, or Mefenoxam + Chlorothalonil. Rotate chemical groups to prevent resistance.
Potato___Late_Blight.recovery_tips: Do not wash potatoes before storing if blight was present in the field. Keep storage relative humidity below 85% and ensure continuous forced-air ventilation.

symptoms: Small, powdery, cinnamon-brown to golden-brown pustules erupting on both top and bottom leaf surfaces.
Pustules turn dark brown to black as the corn plant matures toward harvest.
Severe infections cause leaves to yellow, wither, and die prematurely, resulting in poorly filled ears.
Corn___Common_Rust.causes: Caused by the fungus Puccinia sorghi. Favored by high relative humidity (above 95%) and moderate temperatures (16°C to 25°C).
treatment: Apply foliar fungicides if pustules appear before or during the tasseling/silking stage.
If the crop has already reached the dent or mature dough stage, chemical treatment is generally not economically necessary.
prevention: Plant hybrid corn varieties bred with specific single-leaf (Rp) or adult plant rust resistance.
Plant early in the season to ensure crops pass the vulnerable silking stage before peak summer spore migrations.
Corn___Common_Rust.fungicide: Pyraclostrobin + Metconazole, or Azoxystrobin applied at V8 to VT (tasseling) growth stages.
Corn___Common_Rust.recovery_tips: Ensure adequate potassium supply, which helps regulate stomatal closure and maintains stalk strength to prevent lodging (falling over) in rust-stressed corn.

symptoms: Spindle-shaped or diamond-shaped leaf spots with gray-white centers and brownish-red borders.
Lesions enlarge and coalesce, causing entire leaves to shrivel and turn grey.
Can also attack the node below the grain panicle ('Neck Blast'), causing the entire grain head to fall over and die.
Rice___Leaf_Blast.causes: Caused by the fungus Magnaporthe oryzae. Highly favored by excessive nitrogen fertilizer, stagnant water, and prolonged leaf wetness.
treatment: Drain standing field water for 2-3 days if irrigation control is available, as flooded stagnant water encourages spore proliferation.
Apply systemic anti-blast fungicides immediately upon spotting diamond-shaped lesions.
Split nitrogen fertilizer applications into 3 smaller doses rather than one large basal dumping.
prevention: Burn or plow under infected rice straw and stubble after harvest.
Treat seeds with protective fungicides or biocontrol agents (Bacillus subtilis) before sowing.
Maintain continuous water flow rather than deep stagnant flooding during humid months.
Rice___Leaf_Blast.fungicide: Tricyclazole 75% WP (0.6 g/liter) or Isoprothiolane 40% EC (1.5 ml/liter) applied at active tillering and panicle initiation.
Rice___Leaf_Blast.recovery_tips: Apply a foliar spray of Silicon (Silicic acid or Potassium Silicate), which deposits in rice leaf epidermal cells and forms a hardened barrier against further fungal penetration.
